---
title: "1.2 — Semantics: valuations and truth tables"
---

> **Where you are.** A `Form` is a tree. We now define a function that assigns it a Boolean
> value under a valuation. The final solver will use these calculations, with a proof that
> its finite table covers every valuation relevant to the formula.

## 1. The question: true under which assignment?

Take `(p ∨ q) → q`. With p true and q false it is false; with both false it is true. A formula
with atoms has a value relative to an assignment. A **valuation** is that assignment, represented
by `v : Nat → Bool`. The input is an atom index; the output is its truth value.


```lean
import Principia.Logic.Semantics
open Principia Principia.Form
open scoped Principia.Form Principia
```


```lean
def onlyFirst : Nat → Bool := fun i => i == 0
#eval onlyFirst 0
#eval onlyFirst 1
#eval eval onlyFirst ((Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1) ⇒ Form.var 1)
```

These print `true`, `false`, and `false`. `fun i => ...` defines a function: given an index,
compare it with zero. It assigns false to every other index as well, so it is a complete
valuation even though we only inspect two indices here.

## 2. Reading the evaluator

The supplied `eval` has one equation per constructor:

```text
eval v (var i)   = v i
eval v fls      = false
eval v (imp a b) = (!eval v a) || eval v b
eval v (and a b) = eval v a && eval v b
eval v (or a b)  = eval v a || eval v b
```

`!` reverses a Boolean, `&&` is Boolean and, and `||` is Boolean or. An implication is false
only when its input is true and its output false. Our concrete example evaluates as follows:

```text
p = true; q = false
p or q = true
not (p or q) = false
(not (p or q)) or q = false
```

This is structural recursion on formula data. It doesn't search for a derivation.

We can also reason with unknown children if we know enough about their values:

```lean
example (v : Nat → Bool) (a b : Form) (ha : eval v a = true) :
    eval v (a ⋎ b) = true := by
  simp only [eval]
  rw [ha]
  rfl
```

After unfolding, the goal is `(eval v a || eval v b) = true`. Rewriting `ha` turns the first
input into `true`; `true || x` computes to `true` regardless of the unknown second input.

## 3. A proposition about all valuations

`Tautology a` is defined as `∀ v, eval v a = true`. Its type is `Prop`: it is a claim about
all valuations, not another Boolean or another formula. To prove it, introduce an arbitrary
valuation. For example:

```lean
example (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ b) := by
  intro v
  simp only [eval]
  cases eval v a <;> cases eval v b <;> rfl
```

After `intro v`, we must prove the formula evaluates to true for this arbitrary valuation.
Unfolding leaves `(!(eval v a && eval v b) || eval v b) = true`. There are two Boolean values
to inspect, giving four cases. `<;>` applies the following tactic to every goal produced by
the preceding tactic, so both `cases` commands reach all four combinations. `rfl` computes
each remaining goal. This proves validity for arbitrary formulas a and b.

`Entails Γ a` allows assumptions. Its definition is:

```text
∀ v, (∀ b, b ∈ Γ → eval v b = true) → eval v a = true
```

For example, `Entails [a, a ⇒ b] b` asks about valuations making both listed assumptions
true. An assignment with a false assumption cannot refute that entailment. The notation
`Γ ⊨ a` abbreviates this semantic statement.

## 4. Why a finite table is enough

Although valuations are functions on all natural numbers, any particular formula uses only
finitely many indices. `maxVar a` is an exclusive upper bound: all its indices are smaller.
For `var 3`, the bound is 4, not 1. It is an index bound, not the number of distinct atoms.

```lean
#eval maxVar (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 2)
#eval (allEnvs 2).map (fun v => [v 0, v 1])
#eval taut? ((Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1) ⇒ Form.var 1)
```

The bound printed is 3. The list prints the four assignments to indices 0 and 1. The final
check returns false because p true, q false is a counterexample. `allEnvs n` fixes unused
indices at false and enumerates $2^n$ assignments below n. This can include redundant columns
when atom indices are sparse.

`taut? a` checks `eval v a` for every listed valuation. Later, the final solver uses the
certified theorem `taut?_eq_true_iff a : taut? a = true ↔ Tautology a`. Its proof has two
parts: evaluation ignores indices outside the bound, and the table represents every assignment
inside it. Thus we will connect the executable Boolean check to the universal proposition.

For any atom assignment, `a ⋎ ∼a` evaluates to true by two Boolean cases. This doesn't give
an algorithm deciding an arbitrary Lean proposition `p : Prop`: here we are evaluating finite
formula syntax under assigned Boolean values.

## 5. Keep the three types visible

For the formula `Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1`, consider a valuation assigning false to both atoms:

```lean
#eval eval (fun _ => false) (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1)
```

The output is false. The relevant types have different jobs:

| Expression | Type | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| `Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1` | `Form` | A formula tree. |
| `eval (fun _ => false) (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1)` | `Bool` | Its computed value under this assignment. |
| `eval v a = true` | `Prop` | A claim about one evaluation. |
| `Tautology a` | `Prop` | A claim about every valuation. |

One true row doesn't establish a tautology. One false row is enough to refute it. Checking
that every row in a finite table is true establishes validity only once we have justified
that the table covers all relevant assignments. The final solver will use that coverage proof.


```lean
theorem taut_imp_self (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⇒ φ) := by
  sorry
```

```lean

  sorry
```

## 7. Hints

**`eval_neg`.** Unfold the definition of formula negation and the evaluation equations. A Boolean or with false can be simplified.

**`taut_imp_self`.** Introduce an arbitrary valuation. After unfolding, split on the Boolean value of the subformula.

**`taut_excluded_middle`.** Introduce a valuation and unfold formula negation as well as evaluation. Consider the two Boolean values of the subformula.

## 8. Worked corrections to the required exercises

Try the exercises first. These proofs match `Solution.lean`, checked by `make test`.

### `eval_neg`

```lean
theorem eval_neg (v : Nat → Bool) (φ : Form) : eval v (∼φ) = !eval v φ := by
  simp [Form.neg, eval]
```

Negation expands to implication into falsehood. Unfolding leaves a Boolean negation combined with false, and simplification uses the Boolean identity.

### `taut_imp_self`

```lean
theorem taut_imp_self (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⇒ φ) := by
  intro v; simp only [eval]; cases eval v φ <;> rfl
```

The arbitrary valuation is introduced by the universal quantifier in `Tautology`. The remaining claim depends on one Boolean value. The two branches compute to true.

### `taut_excluded_middle`

```lean
theorem taut_excluded_middle (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⋎ ∼φ) := by
  intro v; simp only [eval, Form.neg]; cases eval v φ <;> rfl
```

The proof again checks a Boolean value, after exposing the derived negation. It proves semantic validity of formula syntax, without deciding arbitrary Lean propositions.

## 10. Worked corrections to the optional exercises

### `eval_top`

```lean
theorem eval_top (v : Nat → Bool) : eval v Form.top = true := by
  simp [Form.top, Form.neg, eval]
```

`top` is negated falsehood, so unfolding gives `(!false) || false`, which computes to true. This statement holds under any valuation because no atom occurs in the formula.


### `taut_and_elim_left`

```lean
theorem taut_and_elim_left (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ a) := by
  intro v
  simp only [eval]
  cases eval v a <;> cases eval v b <;> rfl
```

After introducing v, evaluation leaves `(!(eval v a && eval v b) || eval v a) = true`. The two `cases` commands create the four combinations of the subformula values. Each remaining goal computes. This is the left projection, different from the right projection in the teaching example.


## 11. Conclusion

A valuation supplies Boolean inputs, `eval` combines them, and `Tautology` quantifies over
all valuations. A formula has finitely many relevant indices even though valuations are functions
on every index. The finite table is executable; its certified equivalence will support the solver.
Next we define derivations, keeping semantic truth separate from proof construction.
